source.title: Increasing Computation Resolves Conflicts in Vision Language Models
source.authors: Bing-Yang Wang; Yi-Jiang Li; Yi-Tong Qiao; Maijunxian Wang; Tianwei Zhao; Yuchen Sun; Binyue Deng; Ho-Kin Deng; Nuno Vasconcelos; Dezhi Luo

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how VLM task accuracy and conflict resolution vary with parameter count, using a different outcome and task from language-model cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates 47 VLMs on conflict tasks and reports qualitative performance trends with parameter count. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or test architectural changes at fixed parameter count. Kaplan et al. is cited, but their results are not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study reports VLM accuracy on a new conflict benchmark as a function of parameter count across 47 models. This bears on V6 (downstream performance vs scale) in a new setting. It is a cross-sectional comparison of heterogeneous model families, described only qualitatively from figures, with no fitted curve. V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that larger VLMs resolve conflicts better on standard tasks. On high-conflict tasks, larger models drop below chance on incongruent trials while smaller ones sit at chance, which they read as genuine, human-like resource-dependent conflict processing. They also claim such control emerges from scaling alone, while noting the largest models still do not fully resolve high-conflict tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Measures accuracy on multimodal conflict tasks across VLM parameter sizes; does not measure held-out language-model loss or fit or extrapolate power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported size-related pattern varies with conflict difficulty (standard versus squared/high-conflict) and congruency (congruent versus incongruent).

fits_no_version.finding: OCR/text modality preference in Stroop-object tasks persists across model sizes. 35 of 47 models prefer OCR, and the authors say scaling alone does not remove it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some downstream biases (modality preference) do not change with model scale.

record.problems: The size-related findings are described qualitatively in the text; it provides no fitted predictive relationship or uncertainty estimates for the scaling trend. The paper notes that high-conflict accuracy does not fully recover even for the largest models tested.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant scaling results were reported as separate numerical outcomes in the text. Aggregate congruency effects and modality-preference findings were not included because they do not report the size-related outcome named by V6.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; any fitted or extrapolated relation of accuracy to scale; controlled scaling within a single model family or training recipe.
Not tested; no loss power laws fitted for VLMs.

missing.what: Per-model or size-binned accuracies by congruency for non-squared and squared tasks, plotted against log parameter count
Claim that the size pattern (including the below-chance dip) replicates across all four conflict types
Statement that the largest models' high-conflict accuracy does not fully recover

record.verdict_notes: Scale is varied only across heterogeneous off-the-shelf models (1B–110B plus proprietary models), so parameter count is confounded with family, data and training. No loss is measured and no power law is fitted. The authors cite Kaplan et al. only as motivation for using parameter count as a resource index. The V6 evidence is weak and qualitative. The r4 non-monotonic dip is the most informative result for V6.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.

The study measures accuracy on its own VLM conflict benchmark versus parameter count; it does not test predictability from pretraining loss or establish a general scaling relationship across downstream tasks.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power-law curves.

rows.subject: VLMs (aggregate across tested models)
rows.size_stated: Open-source models range from 1B to 110B parameters; 47 VLMs tested in total.
rows.operation_detail: Compared conflict-task accuracy across models of different parameter counts.
rows.measure: Accuracy as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Smaller models show pronounced congruency effects; larger models exhibit comparable accuracy across congruent and incongruent conditions.
rows.note: Qualitative description; no per-model accuracy values or fitted predictive curve are stated in the text.
rows.check: The text describes the congruency gap shrinking with size but gives no congruent-trial accuracy trend with size. Congruent non-squared accuracy is near ceiling (about 0.95–0.98 mean), so this row cannot show a scale effect on its own measure. The paired gap is better captured by r2.

rows.subject: VLMs (aggregate across tested models)
rows.size_stated: Open-source models range from 1B to 110B parameters; 47 VLMs tested in total.
rows.operation_detail: Compared conflict-task accuracy across models of different parameter counts.
rows.measure: Accuracy as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Smaller models show substantially lower accuracy on incongruent than congruent trials; larger models show comparable accuracy across the two conditions.
rows.note: The prose describes a reduced congruency effect with increased model size, but gives no per-model values or fitted predictive curve.
rows.check: Qualitative only: incongruent accuracy rises toward congruent accuracy with size, read from Figure 4. Parameter count is confounded with model family and training. No per-model values are given in the prose.

rows.operation_detail: Compared conflict-task accuracy across models of different parameter counts.
rows.measure: Accuracy as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Smaller models perform at chance; larger models drop below chance.
rows.note: The authors interpret the below-chance result as evidence of interference and genuine conflict sensitivity, not as improved task accuracy.
rows.check: Accuracy falls from chance to below chance as size grows on squared incongruent trials. This is a non-monotonic, inverse-scaling pattern on a downstream measure. The state is correct; the authors read it as interference, but against V6 it is performance worsening with scale.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.4, lines 738–750; Discussion, lines 781–789; explicit 50% chance labels in Figures 12–13.

relationships.condition: Standard (non-squared) incongruent trials and squared congruent trials, classic conflict tasks
relationships.reason: Larger VLMs close the congruency gap on standard tasks (r2) and rise above chance on squared congruent trials (r3). This is a qualitative cross-model trend only, with no fitted predictive curve.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models narrowed the standard-task congruency gap and rose above chance on squared congruent trials.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Standard (non-squared) incongruent trials and squared congruent trials, classic conflict tasks
source_check.reason: Section 4.4 describes reduced standard-task congruency gaps with size (r2) and squared congruent accuracy moving from chance to above chance (r3). This supports qualitative improvement in these settings; quantitative predictive accuracy is untested.

relationships.reason: Accuracy drops from chance to below chance as parameter count grows (r4), so downstream accuracy does not improve monotonically with scale here.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy dropped from chance to below chance as parameter count increased.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: Section 4.4 explicitly reports smaller models at chance and larger models below chance (r4), reversing the predicted direction of downstream accuracy improvement.

relationships.condition: High-conflict tasks at the largest tested sizes
relationships.reason: The text states the largest models' high-conflict performance does not recover to low-conflict levels. Improvement with scale is therefore incomplete. This verdict is based on the text (Discussion), not on a row.
relationships.display_finding: Even the largest tested models did not recover high-conflict accuracy to low-conflict levels.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: High-conflict tasks at the largest tested sizes
source_check.reason: Discussion, lines 804–810, states that high-conflict accuracy does not recover to low-conflict levels. V6 requires predictable improvement, not complete conflict resolution or equal accuracy across difficulty levels. This residual gap alone does not establish an additional limitation of V6; the reversed scale trend is already captured by l1.

tranche.reason: Own results relate downstream conflict-task accuracy to model size in a new multimodal setting, bearing on V6.

source_check.notes: Scale results are qualitative comparisons across heterogeneous models, without a fitted predictive law or controlled scaling intervention. The pack's auxiliary r1 ceiling range is too broad a characterization: Table 2 gives non-squared congruent Flanker accuracies of 0.873 and 0.859.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard conflict trials and congruent squared high-conflict trials
reader_labels.reason: The study reports a smaller congruency effect in larger models on standard tasks and above-chance congruent performance for larger models where smaller models are at chance (r1–r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Larger models fall below chance while smaller models remain at chance, so increased scale does not produce generally improved accuracy in this condition (r4).
